core: The working definition of a financial goal: a specific outcome a person wants to achieve with money, attributed to the CFPB's goal-setting materials, which distinguish vague dreams from specific goals
Short-, medium-, and long-term goals (under a year, a few years, decades), each with original examples

Goals drive the plan: budgets and saving serve the goals; budgeting and saving referenced only as sibling topics
Trade-offs: every goal competes for the same dollars
Adjusting goals: life changes, goals change; the general practice of revising goals
The honest framing: a goal without a number is a wish

claims.claim: A financial goal is a specific outcome a person wants to achieve with money; the CFPB's goal-setting materials distinguish vague, aspirational dreams from specific, achievable goals.
The CFPB teaches SMART goals — specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound — as a structure that makes goals simpler to plan for, track, and achieve.

Goals sort by time horizon: the CFPB's tool treats goals reachable within about six months as short term and longer goals as long term, and many planners use a three-way split (under a year, a few years, decades).
Setting goals relates to financial decisions: the FDIC's Money Smart curriculum teaches setting short-term and long-term goals for saving and things that affect decisions to spend or save money.

Before you can accomplish a goal you need a plan for how to achieve it; research cited by the CFPB (Dr. Gail Matthews, Dominican University of California) shows people who write down specific goals are much more likely to reach them.
Goals compete for the same dollars; when one goal is critical and cannot be adjusted, other goals may need to be adjusted so the critical one can be funded.

Goals are not set-and-forget: they should be revised as circumstances change (losing or getting a job, earning more, having a child, a health emergency), and when a goal is achieved, the process starts again with a new goal.
The CFPB's Your Money, Your Goals toolkit is a set of financial empowerment materials that help people meet their financial goals by increasing knowledge, skills, and resources.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Time-band boundaries for short-, medium-, and long-term goals differ across frameworks.
positions: The CFPB's SMART-goals tool draws the line at about six months: short term under six months, long term beyond.
Many planners and educators use a three-way split — under a year, a few years, decades — with no universal boundary.
FDIC Money Smart teaches short-term and long-term goals for saving without fixing one boundary.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the three-way split as a common organizing convention with rough bands, anchors the short/long idea in the CFPB's six-month guideline, and never states a band as a rule.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether writing goals down 'causes' goal attainment.
positions: The CFPB's action tool states research shows people who write down specific goals are much more likely to reach them (citing Dr. Gail Matthews).
In other settings the evidence is treated as suggestive rather than causal.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the claim to the research the CFPB cites and phrases it as research cited by the CFPB, not as an absolute law.

sourceRecords.title: Setting SMART goals (Your Money, Your Goals tool)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (U.S. government). Official CFPB PDF downloaded and read on 2026-08-21 via the Your Money, Your Goals toolkit page. Supports: the SMART acronym as Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time bound; SMART structure making goals simpler to plan for, track, and achieve; dreams as aspirational and vague versus goals as specific, achievable things; starting from values so goals are more likely to be prioritized; focusing on one or two priorities; short term (less than six months) versus long term (more than six months); the SMART self-check questions (What will I achieve? How much? Can I actually reach this? Is now the right time? When will I reach this?). Used for the working definition and the SMART framework; facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Revising goals (Your Money, Your Goals handout)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (U.S. government). Official CFPB PDF downloaded and read on 2026-08-21. Supports: goals are not something you can 'set and forget'; revise goals as the situation changes or you may find yourself off track; common reasons to adjust goals include changed circumstances (losing or getting a job, earning more, having a child, a health emergency) and coming up short on a savings goal; when a critical goal cannot be adjusted, adjust other goals so the critical one can be funded; adjusting the total amount or the time frame (e.g., a $600 TV in three months becomes a less expensive TV or a longer timeline); a goal that no longer feels important can be set aside and replaced; setting goals and working toward them is a process that never really ends. Used for the trade-offs and adjusting-goals sections; facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Putting goals into action (Your Money, Your Goals tool)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (U.S. government). Official CFPB PDF downloaded and read on 2026-08-21. Supports: before you can accomplish a goal you need a plan for how to achieve it; an action plan of steps, resources, and deadlines; research (attributed in the tool to Dr. Gail Matthews, Dominican University of California) showing people who write down specific goals are much more likely to reach them; sharing goals with a friend and checking in regularly increases the chances of reaching them. Used for the goals-drive-the-plan section; facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Money Smart for Young People
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (U.S. government). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21.
